passages.happening:
Six days before the Passover, Jesus comes back to Bethany, the village where he raised Lazarus (verse 1). His friends give a dinner for him. Martha serves. Lazarus, who had been dead and was raised, is at the table with him (verse 2).

Then Mary takes about a pint of very costly perfume, “made of pure nard”. She pours it on Jesus' feet and wipes them with her hair. “And the house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume” (verse 3).

Judas Iscariot objects. “Why wasn’t this perfume sold for three hundred denarii and the money given to the poor?” (verse 5). John tells us what was really going on. Judas kept the group's money bag, and he used to help himself from it (verse 6).

Jesus defends her. “Leave her alone,” he says. “She has kept this perfume in preparation for the day of My burial” (verse 7). And then: “The poor you will always have with you, but you will not always have Me” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
At a dinner like this, guests lay on couches around a low table, leaning on one elbow, with their feet stretched out behind them. That is how Mary could reach his feet. The Bible's word for it is ‘reclining’ (verse 2).

Nard was a perfume made from a plant that grows high in the Himalayan mountains. It came a very long way and cost a great deal. A denarius was a day's pay for a laborer (Matthew 20:2), so three hundred denarii was close to a year's wages. Mary poured out something like a year's income in one evening.

She anointed his feet, not his head. Pouring oil on a guest's head was an honor. Feet were the lowest and dirtiest part of the body, and washing them was a servant's job. And she wiped them with her hair. The Mishnah, a book of Jewish teaching written down around AD 200, counts a married woman going out with her head uncovered as against Jewish custom. So many readers think a woman letting down her hair in front of guests was a bold, even shocking, thing to do. Mary did not care what it looked like.

Mark and Matthew tell of an anointing at Bethany too (Mark 14:3-9, Matthew 26:6-13), and their notes explain it. There a woman who is not named pours perfume on Jesus' head, in the house of Simon the Leper, and several disciples object. John names her as Mary and names Judas as the one who objects. Many readers think the Gospels tell the same evening, each with its own details; a woman could anoint both head and feet. Others think there were two different anointings. Luke tells a different story, earlier, in Galilee, of a ‘sinful woman’ who weeps on Jesus' feet (Luke 7:36-50).

This Mary is Lazarus's sister (11:2), not Mary Magdalene, and not the woman of Luke 7. In the West, from a sermon by Pope Gregory the Great in 591, the three women were often blended into one, and she was preached as a reformed sinner. The Eastern churches always kept them apart. In 2021 the Catholic Church gave Martha, Mary and Lazarus a shared feast day, 29 July. John says nothing about Mary's past. He shows her love.
passages.ot:
Jesus' words about the poor come from the law of Moses. In Deuteronomy 15, God tells Israel never to “harden your heart or shut your hand from your poor brother” (Deuteronomy 15:7). Then he says, “For there will never cease to be poor in the land; that is why I am commanding you to open wide your hand to your brother and to the poor and needy in your land” (Deuteronomy 15:11). In Moses' law, the fact that the poor will always be there is the reason to give, not the excuse not to.

Anointing was how Israel's kings were marked out. And a psalm of trust says to God, “You anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows” (Psalm 23:5).
passages.hard:
Does ‘the poor you will always have with you’ mean poverty does not matter? People have used the verse that way: as a reason to shrug at the poor, or to spend money on fine things instead of on people in need. That reading is wrong, and it turns Jesus' words upside down.

First, Jesus is quoting Deuteronomy 15:11, and that verse is a command to give freely, because the poor will always be among God's people. Second, Mark's account adds his words, “and you can help them whenever you want” (Mark 14:7). Third, he is speaking about one unique moment. In a few days he will die. Mary saw it, and acted while she could. Fourth, John himself takes for granted that Jesus and his friends gave to the poor. When Judas leaves the supper, some disciples think Jesus has sent him “to give something to the poor” (13:29).

So the verse does not set Jesus against the poor. It says that love for Jesus and care for the poor belong together, and that this one evening called for this one gift. Jesus, who praised Mary's gift, is the same one who said that whatever is done for the hungry is done for him (Matthew 25:40).
passages.asks: Mary gave her best, all at once, and someone called it a waste. Judas talked about the poor, but he loved money. Ask which voice is louder in you: the one that counts the cost, or the one that wants to give Jesus something precious. And ask whether your love for him shows itself, as Deuteronomy commands, in an open hand to people in need.

passages.happening:
Word gets out that Jesus is in Bethany. A large crowd comes, not only to see Jesus, but to see Lazarus, the man who had been dead (verse 9).

So the chief priests make plans to kill Lazarus as well (verse 10). The reason is simple: “for on account of him many of the Jews were deserting them and believing in Jesus” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
In chapter 11 the council had already decided that Jesus must die (11:53). The priests feared that if people kept believing in him, ‘the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation’ (11:48). Now Lazarus himself has become a problem. A man walking around alive after four days in the tomb was the best evidence there could be.

‘The Jews’ here means many ordinary Jewish people from Jerusalem and the villages who came to believe. John is not speaking against the Jewish people. He is saying that many of them believed, and that their leaders were afraid of losing them. The book page explains how John uses the phrase.

The chief priests were the leading families of the temple, from whom the high priest was chosen. The high priest held his office with Rome's approval, and could lose it.
passages.ot: The prophets knew what it was to be hated for the truth. When God called Jeremiah, he warned him that his own people would oppose him: “They will fight against you but will never overcome you, since I am with you to deliver you” (Jeremiah 1:19).
passages.asks: Lazarus did nothing but live, and that was enough to make him a target. Sometimes a changed life is the most troubling sermon there is. Ask whether your own life shows that Jesus has done something in it. And if you are paying a price simply for being who Jesus made you, remember that Lazarus paid it first, standing next to the one who gave him life.

passages.t: The king comes on a donkey
passages.happening:
The next day, the great crowd in Jerusalem for the feast hears that Jesus is coming. They take palm branches and go out to meet him. They shout, “Hosanna!” “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Blessed is the King of Israel!” (verse 13).

Jesus finds a young donkey and sits on it. John says this fulfils Scripture: “Do not be afraid, O Daughter of Zion. See, your King is coming, seated on the colt of a donkey” (verse 15).

At first the disciples did not understand. Only after Jesus was glorified, after his death and rising, did they remember and see that these things had been written about him (verse 16). The crowd that had seen Lazarus raised kept telling what they had seen (verses 17-18). The Pharisees say to one another, “Look how the whole world has gone after Him!” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
Palm branches meant victory for a nation. When Simon Maccabeus took back the fortress in Jerusalem from foreign troops in 141 BC, his people entered it with palm branches and songs (1 Maccabees 13:51). Only John says the branches were palms. A crowd waving palms at Passover, hailing a ‘King of Israel’, could easily alarm the Roman soldiers in the city.

‘Hosanna’ comes from Hebrew words in Psalm 118:25 that mean ‘save, please’. Over time it also became a shout of praise. Psalm 118 was one of the psalms sung at the great feasts, so pilgrims knew it by heart.

‘Went out to meet Him’ describes how a city often welcomed an important visitor. People went out of the gates and escorted him in. But Jesus does not come on a war horse. He comes on a young donkey. That is the point. He is a king, but not the kind of king the crowd may have hoped for.

John lets the Pharisees say more than they know. ‘The whole world has gone after Him’, they complain. In the very next verse, people from other nations come looking for him.
passages.ot:
The crowd's words come from Psalm 118: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD” (Psalm 118:26). The same psalm speaks of “The stone the builders rejected” that “has become the cornerstone” (Psalm 118:22).

The donkey comes from Zechariah: “See, your King comes to you, righteous and victorious, humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9). The next verse says this king will take away the war horse and “proclaim peace to the nations” (Zechariah 9:10). John opens the quotation with ‘Do not be afraid’, which may echo Zephaniah, where God says to Jerusalem, “Israel’s King, the LORD, is among you” (Zephaniah 3:15). King Solomon rode David's mule to be made king (1 Kings 1:33).
passages.asks: The crowd welcomed a king, but the disciples only understood afterward what kind of king he was. Ask what kind of king you are hoping Jesus will be: one who wins your battles for you, or one who comes humble, bringing peace. And notice that the disciples understood later, looking back. It is not a failure to understand something about Jesus only years afterward.

passages.happening:
Some Greeks have come up to worship at the feast. They come to Philip, who is from Bethsaida in Galilee, and ask, “Sir, we want to see Jesus” (verse 21). Philip tells Andrew, and the two of them tell Jesus.

Jesus' answer seems at first not to answer them at all. “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified” (verse 23). Then he gives a picture: “unless a kernel of wheat falls to the ground and dies, it remains only a seed; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (verse 24).

He goes on: “Whoever loves his life will lose it, but whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life” (verse 25). Anyone who serves him must follow him, and where he is, his servant will be too. “If anyone serves Me, the Father will honor him” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
These Greeks were not Jews who spoke Greek. They were Gentiles, people of other nations, who had come to worship Israel's God at the feast. They could stand in the great outer court of the temple, but no further. A low wall kept them out of the inner courts, with signs warning that a foreigner who went past it would be to blame for his own death. One of those signs was found in Jerusalem in 1871.

Philip and Andrew both have Greek names, and both come from Bethsaida (1:44). Perhaps that is why the visitors came to them.

‘The hour’ is a key phrase in John. All through the first half of the book Jesus has said his hour had not yet come (2:4, 7:30, 8:20). Now, when people from the nations come asking for him, he says it has come. In John the hour means his death, his rising, and his return to the Father.

‘Hates his life’ is a Hebrew way of saying ‘loves it less’. Genesis says Jacob ‘loved Rachel more than Leah’, and the next verse calls Leah ‘unloved’; the King James Version has ‘hated’ (Genesis 29:30-31). Jesus is not asking anyone to despise themselves. He is asking them to love following him more than anything, even life.

The grain of wheat has spoken far beyond the church. The Russian novelist Fyodor Dostoevsky put verse 24 at the front of The Brothers Karamazov, published in 1880.
passages.ot:
The prophets looked for the day when the nations would come to Israel's God. Isaiah says, “Many peoples will come and say, ‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD’” (Isaiah 2:3). Now the nations are asking for Jesus, and he says that the way to them runs through his death.

The picture of life coming through death is in the Old Testament too. Isaiah says of the suffering Servant that after his suffering “He will see His offspring, He will prolong His days” (Isaiah 53:10).
passages.hard:
Is ‘whoever hates his life’ a call to self-hatred? No. ‘Hate’ here is a Hebrew way of saying ‘love less’. Matthew gives the same saying as loving father or mother ‘more than Me’ (Matthew 10:37). The verse is about what comes first, not about despising yourself or neglecting your body.

If you are struggling with thoughts of not wanting to live, please hear this plainly: this verse is not about that, and it gives no permission for it. Jesus came so that his sheep “may have life, and have it in all its fullness” (10:10). A doctor, a counselor, medicine, one trusted person who will stay. If you have reached the place where you are not sure you want to be here at all, tell someone today, and in the United States you can call or text 988 right now.
passages.asks: A seed kept safe in a jar stays a seed. Only buried does it become a harvest. Jesus said this first of his own death. Then he said it of everyone who follows him. Ask what you are holding onto so tightly that it cannot bear fruit. And remember the promise at the end: where he is, his servant will be, and the Father will honor that servant.

passages.happening:
Jesus says, “Now My soul is troubled, and what shall I say? ‘Father, save Me from this hour’? No, it is for this purpose that I have come to this hour. Father, glorify Your name!” (verses 27-28).

A voice comes from heaven: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again” (verse 28). Some in the crowd say it thundered. Others say an angel spoke to him. Jesus says the voice was for their sake, not his (verses 29-30).

Then he says, “Now judgment is upon this world; now the prince of this world will be cast out. And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw everyone to Myself” (verses 31-32). John explains: “He said this to indicate the kind of death He was going to die” (verse 33).

The crowd is puzzled. The Law, they say, teaches that the Christ will remain forever. So how can the Son of Man be lifted up? “Who is this Son of Man?” (verse 34). Jesus answers that the light will be with them only a little longer. “While you have the Light, believe in the Light, so that you may become sons of light” (verse 36). Then he goes away and hides from them.
passages.hearers:
Matthew, Mark and Luke tell of Jesus praying in the garden of Gethsemane the night before he died. His soul was ‘consumed with sorrow’, and he prayed that ‘the hour would pass from Him’ (Mark 14:34-35). John does not tell the garden prayer. But here, days earlier, he shows the same struggle: a troubled soul, a prayer about the hour, and a yes to the Father.

‘Lifted up’ is one of John's words with two meanings, as the book page explains. It can mean raised high in honor, or raised up on a cross. John says Jesus meant his death (verse 33), and the reader is meant to hear both. The cross is where he is raised high.

The crowd's question makes sense. Many Jews hoped for a Messiah who would reign for ever, as God promised David (Psalm 89:36). A Messiah who dies did not fit. That is still the question at the heart of the faith.

‘Prince of this world’ means the devil, the power of evil at work in the world. Jesus says the cross is where that power is thrown down. ‘Sons of light’ means people who belong to the light. A Jewish community of the time, at Qumran by the Dead Sea, called its members by the same name.
passages.ot:
‘Lifted up’ echoes the bronze snake that Moses set on a pole in the desert, so that people who looked at it lived (Numbers 21:9). Jesus used that picture with Nicodemus (3:14).

It also echoes Isaiah's suffering Servant: “Behold, My Servant will prosper; He will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted” (Isaiah 52:13). The same Servant is then “pierced for our transgressions” (Isaiah 53:5). Isaiah puts the lifting high and the suffering side by side, as John does.

A voice that sounds like thunder recalls Mount Sinai, where “Moses spoke and God answered him in the thunder” (Exodus 19:19).
passages.hard:
Does ‘I will draw everyone to Myself’ mean that every person will be saved? Christians read it in different ways. Many read ‘everyone’ as all kinds of people, Greeks as well as Jews, which fits the Greeks who have just come asking for him. Others read it as Jesus drawing every person toward him, though not all will come. A smaller number of Christians, in several traditions, have hoped from verses like this that in the end all will be saved. John's own book also says plainly that people can refuse the light (3:19). These notes do not settle it.

And was Jesus afraid? His soul was ‘troubled’, the same word John uses at Lazarus's tomb (11:33). He was not pretending. The church confesses that Jesus is truly God and truly man, and here we see the man, shaken, and still saying yes.
passages.asks: Jesus did not hide that he was troubled. He said so out loud, and then he prayed. If you are facing something you dread, his words give you permission to be honest about the fear, and they show you where to take it. Ask what it would look like to pray as he did: not ‘take this away’ only, but ‘Father, glorify Your name’ in this.

passages.happening:
Now John looks back over everything Jesus has done in public. “Although Jesus had performed so many signs in their presence, they still did not believe in Him” (verse 37).

John says this fulfilled Isaiah: “Lord, who has believed our message? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (verse 38). And: “He has blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts, so that they cannot see with their eyes, and understand with their hearts, and turn, and I would heal them” (verse 40). John adds, “Isaiah said these things because he saw Jesus’ glory and spoke about Him” (verse 41).

But then: “Nevertheless, many of the leaders believed in Him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess Him, for fear that they would be put out of the synagogue” (verse 42). “For they loved praise from men more than praise from God” (verse 43).
passages.hearers:
The first readers of John may have been asking a painful question. If Jesus really was the Messiah, why did so many of his own people, and so many others, not believe? John's answer is that Scripture had seen it coming. The prophets were often not believed either.

To be ‘put out of the synagogue’ was a heavy cost. The synagogue was the center of a town's life: its prayer, its reading of Scripture, its friendships and its help in hard times. The book page and the note on 9:22 explain what historians say about this. Many scholars think John's book was finished in a time of painful separation. Others think local exclusions like this could have happened in Jesus' own lifetime. Either way, John describes particular leaders and particular fears.

Notice that the leaders who believed were Jews, and that John says ‘many’ of them believed. These verses are not a verdict on the Jewish people. They have sometimes been preached that way, and that is wrong. They describe what any person can do: see the light and look away, or believe in secret because of what others will say.
passages.ot:
Both quotations come from Isaiah. The first is Isaiah 53:1, about the Servant: “Who has believed our message? And to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?” (Isaiah 53:1). The second is from Isaiah 6, when God calls the prophet. There God tells Isaiah to “Make the hearts of this people calloused; deafen their ears and close their eyes” (Isaiah 6:10). In that chapter Isaiah sees ‘the Lord seated on a throne, high and exalted’ (Isaiah 6:1). And Isaiah 52:13 uses the same words, ‘lifted up and highly exalted’, for the Servant. John joins the two. The Lord Isaiah saw on the throne and the Servant who suffers are both, John says, about Jesus.

Mark and Matthew quote the same lines from Isaiah 6 about Jesus' parables (Mark 4:12, Matthew 13:14-15), and their notes face the same question.
passages.hard:
If God blinded their eyes, how can they be blamed for not believing? On its plainest reading, verse 39, ‘For this reason they were unable to believe’, can sound that way, and readers have felt the difficulty from the start.

Christians have answered in different ways. John Chrysostom, a preacher of the late 300s, said the ‘because’ points to what was going to happen, not to its cause: Isaiah did not make them disbelieve; he spoke because they were not going to believe. He also said that ‘could not’ here stands for ‘would not’. Augustine gave a similar answer: if asked why they could not believe, he said, because they would not, and God foresaw it. Christians in the tradition that stresses God's choosing hold that God truly hardens, but as a just judgment on hearts already turned away, so that the guilt is still theirs. Many others stress that in Isaiah the hardening came after long refusal. Christians who stress God's choosing and those who stress human freedom have read these verses differently for centuries. These notes do not settle it.

What John does is plain. Straight after the quotation he says many leaders did believe (verse 42). And straight after that, Jesus cries out again, inviting people to believe (verses 44-46). The door is not shut. If you are afraid that your doubts mean God has shut you out, notice that this passage is followed by an invitation.
passages.asks: Some of the leaders believed, but kept quiet, because they loved the praise of people more than the praise of God. That is a mirror for every reader. Ask where the fear of what others think keeps you silent about what you believe. For some people, in some places, speaking up carries real danger; John is honest about the cost. But ask whose approval you are living for.

passages.t: Not to judge the world, but to save it
passages.happening:
Jesus cries out one last time in public. “Whoever believes in Me does not believe in Me alone, but in the One who sent Me. And whoever sees Me sees the One who sent Me” (verses 44-45).

“I have come into the world as a light, so that no one who believes in Me should remain in darkness” (verse 46). Then: “As for anyone who hears My words and does not keep them, I do not judge him. For I have not come to judge the world, but to save the world” (verse 47).

Yet there is a judge. The word Jesus has spoken will judge the one who rejects him on the last day (verse 48). He has not spoken on his own. The Father told him what to say, “And I know that His command leads to eternal life” (verse 50).
passages.hearers:
John has just said that Jesus hid himself (verse 36). So these last words have no new scene. Many readers think John gathers here, as a summary, what Jesus has said all through the first half of the book: believing, seeing, being sent, light and darkness, judgment, and life.

In the ancient world, a messenger sent by a king spoke with the king's own authority. To receive the messenger was to receive the king. Jesus speaks this way about himself and the Father. But he says more than a messenger could: ‘whoever sees Me sees the One who sent Me’.

This is the last time Jesus speaks to the crowds in John's book. From chapter 13 on, he speaks to his own disciples.
passages.ot: God promised Moses a prophet like him: “I will put My words in his mouth, and he will tell them everything I command him” (Deuteronomy 18:18). The next verse warns that God himself will call to account anyone who will not listen to that prophet's words (Deuteronomy 18:19). Jesus says the same: he speaks what the Father commands, and that word will judge.
passages.hard: How can Jesus say he does not judge, and also that his word will judge? Both are true in John. He came to save, not to condemn: “For God did not send His Son into the world to condemn the world, but to save the world through Him” (3:17). But light shows what is in the dark. The one who turns away from it is judged by the very word that was offered to save him (3:18-19). The judgment is not Jesus' wish. It is what refusing the light means.
passages.asks: Jesus' last public words are an invitation, not a threat. He came as light, so that no one who believes need stay in the dark. Ask where you are still sitting in the dark when the light is right there. The word that could judge you is the same word that offers you eternal life.
